sections.h2: Where deeds and liens are recorded
sections.html:
The Recordings Division of the Bexar County Clerk files and keeps real property records, personal property records, notices of trustee sale and public notices. To file in person, go to the Paul Elizondo Tower, 101 W. Nueva, Suite 103, San Antonio 78205, phone 210-335-2581. A Southside Annex inside Precinct 1 at 3505 Pleasanton Rd. also takes filings, at 210-335-3522.

Doors open at 8 a.m. on weekdays and close at 5 p.m., with a later 5:45 closing on Wednesdays. The Deed Records desk, which pulls copies and researches liens, is in Suite B109 of the same tower at 210-335-2273. Mail goes to the Clerk's Office, Attn: Recordings, 100 Dolorosa, Suite 104, San Antonio.

Each month a "Records on the Run" satellite office moves between precinct offices and community centers, which can save a downtown trip. The clerk also runs a Vanguard Property Alert that warns owners about potentially fraudulent filings, and accepts wills for safekeeping.

A single page costs $25.00 to record, and each extra page adds $4.00. The first-page charge breaks into a $5.00 recording fee, a $10.00 records archive fee and a $10.00 records management fee, all effective January 1, 2024.

The clerk's fee page lists every total from 1 through 50 pages. Add-ons you are most likely to meet:

  • Notice of trustee sale: $2.00 filing, $1.00 for a plain copy
  • Federal tax lien instruments: $30.00 total
  • Plats: $81.00 total per mylar
  • Deed copies: $1.00 per page plus $5.00 per certification
  • Electronic copy of an electronic document: $1.00 up to 10 pages, then $0.10 per page

Bring originals bearing original signatures; copies are refused. Staff cashier each document, assign an instrument number and scan it while you wait, then hand back or return the original. Accepted payment is cash, credit card, check or money order, with checks made out to the Bexar County Clerk.

E-filing is its own lane. Local Government Code section 195.003 reserves it for attorneys, banks and credit unions, federally backed mortgage lenders, persons approved to make regulated loans, title companies, state agencies and municipal clerks. The clerk approves six providers, including CSC, Simplifile, ePN, Indecomm and Hopdox.

Staff will not draft a deed or vouch for clear title, and they refer anyone wanting assurance to a title company or attorney. Property Code 12.001(b) also requires a conveyance to be signed and acknowledged before a notary or similar officer before it is recorded.

sections.h2: Checking for liens before you sell
sections.html:
Try the clerk's public records search first, or stop at the Deed Records Department, Suite B109 of the Paul Elizondo Tower, where staff can direct you to recorded liens on a property. The clerk does not guarantee clear title and takes no responsibility for encumbrances, so a guaranteed search comes from a title company, with an attorney as the other route.

Mortgage foreclosure notices can be pulled from the same search. A list is also available through the clerk's GIS Foreclosure Map or at the Deed Records counter. For the tax foreclosure list, call the law firm that handles those cases at 210-225-4422.

  • Release of lien: record the original in person at the tower or mail it to the courthouse office, at $25.00 for the first page
  • Lost deed: a certified copy runs $1.00 per page plus $5.00 per certification
  • Plain copies: found online under Land Records in the Official Public Records Search

For a seller, the practical order is simple. Search the records for your name and address, request payoff letters for any lien that appears, and ask for a tax certificate. Bring the payoff letters to the title company so each item can be released at closing. If a release was never recorded after an old loan was paid, the lender can record one, and the clerk's index will show it once it is filed. Resolve this before an offer, so the closing date is not at risk.

Run this check before listing, since a lien you did not know about can stall a contract. Cash buyers want clean title too, so the same search applies to a quick cash sale.

Public cash auctions for mortgage and tax foreclosures take place on the first Tuesday of every month, 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. When that Tuesday falls on January 1 or July 4, the sale moves to Wednesday. Bidding happens outdoors beside the courthouse, in the gap between it and the Paul Elizondo Tower, unless Commissioners Court names a different spot.

Bidders need no registration for a mortgage foreclosure, but registration is required to bid on a tax foreclosure. Only cash or certified funds work, and personal checks are refused. A GIS Foreclosure Map tracks notices and is refreshed twice a month, on the first Friday after the auction and about 18 days before the next sale.

An owner can buy back agricultural or homestead property within two years, and other property within six months, with the clock running from the day the sale deed is recorded. A free foreclosure training seminar meets on each first Tuesday. Notice of a sale has to be posted and filed with the clerk 21 or more days before it.

Bexar County had an estimated 2,160,088 residents in mid-2025, 7.5 percent above the 2020 base, in 853,619 housing units. Owners live in 58.8 percent of occupied homes. A typical owned home is valued at $262,200, and typical monthly rent is $1,354.

Two offices split the tax work: the Bexar Central Appraisal District handles valuation and protests, and the Bexar County Tax Assessor-Collector takes payments. BCAD takes no tax payments. It mails value notices to new owners and to anyone whose market value climbed $1,000 or more, and a protest can be filed without a notice.

For tax certificates and payment questions, call 210-335-6628, at the Vista Verde Plaza Building. Across Texas, value is fixed each January 1, bills arrive in October, and unpaid tax turns delinquent February 1. School districts exempt $140,000 of a homestead, and seniors or disabled owners receive $60,000 on top.

Mind the lien. Each January 1 the year's tax lien attaches to the land, so a closing agent will ask for a current tax certificate and proof that earlier years are paid. Order the certificate early in the sale so a surprise balance does not delay closing.

faqs.q: What is the first-page fee for a deed?
faqs.a: The total is $25.00, built from a $5.00 recording fee and two $10.00 charges, one for the archive and one for records management. Pages after the first cost $4.00 each.

faqs.q: Will the clerk record a photocopy of my deed?
faqs.a: No. Only the signed original is accepted. Take it to the Paul Elizondo Tower or mail it to the courthouse office.

faqs.q: Which day are foreclosure auctions held?
faqs.a: Monthly, on the first Tuesday, with bidding from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. A first Tuesday that lands on January 1 or July 4 pushes the sale to Wednesday.

faqs.q: Can I order a certified deed copy by mail?
faqs.a: Yes. Write to the clerk's courthouse office, or ask at the Deed Records Department inside the Paul Elizondo Tower. Expect $1.00 a page plus $5.00 for certification.

faqs.q: Does the appraisal district collect property tax?
faqs.a: No. Its work is values, exemptions and protests. For payments and tax certificates, call the Bexar County Tax Assessor-Collector at 210-335-6628.
